The Adversarial RL Loop:
a prompt engineering and optimisation technique
by iterative exploration of prompt space

Samuele Stronati

Abstract

Writing a prompt that really does what one wants is a search: one starts from a first formulation and changes it until it comes close to a target prompt that no one knows in advance. The Adversarial RL Loop is a multi-agent heuristic for this search, in which each iteration is a semantic operation on the prompt and a judge estimates the direction of the step from the outcomes of adversarial testers; its division of roles is inspired by reinforcement learning, although no parameters are trained. A compiler, in its simplest form an LLM call rather than a translator between languages, writes a candidate from the target and the accumulated fixes; isolated testers, each prompted to break one constraint, see only their part of it; a judge that never sees the candidate reads the verdicts and the verdict–fix history and writes the next fix. Because the loop asks of the compiler only that it map the target and the fixes to a candidate, the compiler can also be any existing prompt-engineering technique encoded in that form, which the loop then wraps with the aim of helping it converge. We state the information flow as per-role receive-sets, correct the history to verdict–fix pairs, and give four plain statements about cost, halting, the budget and pointer fixes. Two live runs, selected examples rather than an evaluation (𝑛=2, no baseline), ended with every tester passing after 4 and 3 iterations. In the longer run, a fix that stopped a leak dropped a confidential note; the judge traced the alternation in the history to a shared word budget, and after its third fix all five testers passed.

1 Introduction

Writing a good prompt is largely a search. One starts from a first formulation and changes it one step at a time, hoping that each change brings it closer to the formulation that would really do what we want and that does not exist yet. We can picture all possible formulations as points of the semantic space in which the model interprets them, and the ideal prompt as one point of that space, the target prompt. The point is hypothetical, since no one knows it in advance, but it gives the search its meaning: every change is a semantic operation that moves the prompt, and a good procedure is one that moves it in the right direction.

The Adversarial RL Loop is a heuristic for carrying out this search in a structured way. At each iteration the current prompt, which we call the candidate, is put to the test by a set of testers, each attending to one aspect of the target, and a judge reads their outcomes together with the history of earlier attempts, estimates how far the candidate still is from the point sought and chooses the operation that should bring it closer, a fix written in natural language. The compiler applies the fix and produces the next candidate, and the cycle repeats until the testers have nothing left to object to or the iteration budget runs out. No one measures the distance to the target prompt directly: the judge estimates it from the testers’ outcomes, and that estimate drives the heuristic.

A familiar example is gradient descent, which looks for the parameters that minimise a loss function by taking steps, each in the direction in which the loss falls fastest, without knowing the end point in advance. Our loop proceeds in the same way in prompt space, where the quantity to reduce is the semantic distance from the target prompt and the judge’s diagnosis takes the place of the gradient in giving the direction of the step, although that distance cannot be differentiated and nothing guarantees that every step reduces it. The analogy has already been used in prompt optimisation by ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023) and TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025), which call “gradient” the textual critique written by an LLM that reads the prompt and the errors it produced. Our loop differs from them in the two traits that give it its name. It is adversarial, because the direction comes from testers that actively try to make the candidate fail, each on one constraint, rather than from errors on a given set of examples; and it is inspired by reinforcement learning, because the candidate is put to the test in an environment, the verdicts act as a reward and the judge, like a critic, estimates from the outcomes how far the target still is without ever reading the prompt, although no parameter is updated (Section 2).

The search becomes harder when aspects of the target interact. A system prompt, for example, must resist prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023) while staying useful, and a change that makes it safer can make it less useful. We call constraints coupled when a fix that satisfies one of them tends to break another, and under coupled constraints approaching the target one constraint at a time can make the candidate oscillate: the fix for 𝐴 breaks 𝐵, and the fix for 𝐵 breaks 𝐴 again. In gradient descent the same phenomenon is the zig-zag along a narrow valley (Section 2.6). Figure 1 sets it beside the loop’s split, which gives each constraint to an isolated tester and the fix to a judge that knows the history of attempts.

The loop separates generation from verification. Generation is the harder step in the sense that one candidate must satisfy all constraints jointly, whereas each check concerns a single constraint. The loop is built on an assumed asymmetry: checking one constraint on a given candidate is expected to be cheaper than producing a candidate that satisfies all constraints jointly (Figure 2). We do not measure this asymmetry; prior work uses a similar asymmetry when it trains verifiers to rank generated solutions (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), and tool- or execution-grounded critique (Gou et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024) relies on external checks, which matters because intrinsic self-correction without them can fail (Huang et al., 2024). Where no cheap check exists, the loop has no asymmetry to exploit and we do not recommend it.

We call 𝐶 the compiler because it turns a specification into an artefact, although in its simplest form it is a stochastic LLM call, not a deterministic translator between languages. Each role is a separate LLM agent that receives only what it needs. The testers, isolated from one another, are adversarial in stance, each trying to break the candidate on a single constraint, but no tester is trained and the loop solves no min-max game; the judge never sees the candidate and knows only the testers’ outcomes.

The loop uses only the compiler’s interface: the target and the fixes go in, a candidate comes out. When the compiler is a plain LLM driven by its role prompt, the loop is a prompt-engineering technique in its own right; in its place can sit any known technique that can be encoded as a compiler with that signature. The loop then becomes a wrapper around that technique, in the systems-engineering sense: it leaves the technique’s workings unchanged and surrounds it with isolated testers and a history-reading judge, with the aim of helping the technique, and the prompts it generates, converge on the target. The direction of that convergence comes first from the compiler: a specialised one is reinforced in its own direction, and with a general one the user’s target sets it (Section 3.1).

Among the closest methods, the difference lies in the separation of roles. In Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) one model generates, critiques and refines; in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation (Zheng et al., 2023) the judge grades, whereas here the testers grade and the judge diagnoses their verdicts and writes the next fix. Pooling several checkers’ critiques into feedback for the generator is shared with LLM-Modulo (Kambhampati et al., 2024), and the synthesise–verify cycle with CEGIS (Solar-Lezama et al., 2006). By “converged” or “halted” we mean only that the loop stopped with halt(𝑣)=𝗒𝖾𝗌, that is, every tester passed in that iteration; we give no unconditional convergence guarantee, and the conditional theorem of Section 6 rests on assumptions about the judge that we do not verify.

We define the history as the sequence 𝐻𝑛=((𝑣1,𝑓1),...,(𝑣𝑛,𝑓𝑛)) of verdict vectors and fixes; the judge reads 𝐻𝑛 and the compiler reads only its fix projection 𝜋𝐹(𝐻𝑛)=(𝑓1,...,𝑓𝑛). This corrects 𝐻←𝐻∪{𝑓} in the source note, the technical note this work starts from (below, “the note”). The judge’s accumulated history is meant to counter oscillation, much as Reflexion carries verbal feedback across trials in an episodic memory (Shinn et al., 2023). Reading it, the judge can notice that two tests fail in turn and write one fix meant for both.

Our contributions are (i) a reading of the loop as a heuristic search in prompt space, in which each fix is a step towards a hypothetical target prompt and the judge estimates its direction from the outcomes of adversarial testers (Section 2); (ii) an information-flow discipline stated as per-role receive-sets: testers see only their projection (the part of the candidate they are given) and never each other, the judge never sees the candidate but reads the whole verdict–fix history, and the compiler sees only the target and the fixes (Section 4); (iii) the loop as a wrapper: because the compiler is defined only by its interface, any prompt-engineering technique encoded as a compiler can run inside the loop, which is meant as an aid to its convergence (Section 3.1); (iv) a small corrected model and four plain statements, each with a one-sentence justification, plus a convergence theorem under explicit assumptions (Sections 5 and 6); (v) two worked runs with transcripts that show the loop iteration by iteration, from the first candidate to the final solution (Section 7): in the first the judge resolves an oscillation between two constraints, and the second shows why the judge must write out in full what it wants to keep; (vi) a barrier report as a defined outcome, framed as diagnosis, not proof (Section 6). We claim no novelty for the loop as such and no empirical superiority over related methods (see the related-work notes at the end).

2 Search in prompt space

2.1 The target prompt and the acceptance region

Let 𝑆 be the space of prompts, that is, of all the candidates the compiler can write, and give it the geometry that comes from the model that reads them: two prompts are close when the model reads them in a similar way and is guided by them in a similar way, and far apart when it draws different behaviour from them. In this space the target prompt 𝑠† is the point that fully realises the target 𝑃, and the quantity the loop tries to reduce is the semantic distance 𝑑(𝑠𝑛,𝑠†) between the current candidate and that point. Neither the point nor the distance is observable. The target prompt is hypothetical in the way that, in supervised learning, the function a model tries to approximate is hypothetical, and it gives the search a direction rather than a measure of its progress.

What is observable is the testers’ verdicts. Each tester splits the space into the candidates it passes and those it fails, and the intersection of the passed parts is the acceptance region 𝐴={𝑠∈𝑆:𝐿(𝑠)=0}, where the loss 𝐿 counts the testers that fail the candidate (Section 5). The loop halts when the candidate enters 𝐴, not when it reaches 𝑠† (Figure 3). If the testers represent the target well, 𝐴 is a small neighbourhood of the target prompt and halting in 𝐴 means having come close to it; if they represent it poorly, 𝐴 can contain points far from 𝑠†, and this is the precise sense in which halting is sound only relative to the testers. The loss is therefore a coarse indicator of the distance: it is zero in 𝐴, but it does not tell apart two candidates that fail the same number of tests while lying at very different distances from the target.

2.2 Each iteration is a semantic operation

A fix is an instruction in natural language, such as adding a rule, narrowing a sentence or moving a note, which the compiler turns into a new candidate. In prompt space it is therefore a step, an operation on the prompt’s meaning that moves it from one point to another and that, as the heuristic intends, brings it closer to the target prompt. Unlike a numerical step, though, the new position is not obtained by adding the last step to the previous position. The compiler does not see the previous candidate and rewrites the prompt each time from the target and all the accumulated fixes, 𝑠𝑛+1=𝐶(𝑃,(𝑓1,...,𝑓𝑛)), so the candidate depends on the whole path and not only on the last step. This is why a fix must describe its step in self-contained terms, since an operation that points at the current candidate, such as “leave the rest unchanged”, has nothing to apply to (Section 5); for the same reason the path accumulates as a sequence of constraints on the prompt’s meaning, which the compiler rereads in full at every iteration.

2.3 How the judge estimates distance and direction

The judge never sees the candidate, so it cannot measure where it is. It reconstructs that from what the testers report, which are so many partial observations of the candidate, each made from a different point of view and limited to its own projection. A tester that fails the candidate says that it lies on the wrong side of a boundary, and its reason says where, that is, which part of the prompt gave way and how. The judge combines these indications into an estimate: how many and which testers fail gives it an idea of how far the candidate still is from 𝐴, the reasons tell it which way to move it, and the fix it writes is the resulting step (Figure 4).

The history adds the dimension of time to this estimate. In the sequence of verdicts and fixes the judge sees how the candidate moved in response to each step, which directions brought it closer and which took it back to where it had already been, and it can correct the estimate of the moment with the experience of earlier iterations. This is where the heuristic differs from a reaction to the last failure: the direction of the next step depends on the whole trajectory, and a step that once reopened a failure already closed weighs on the choice of the new one. Nothing forces the judge to use the history in this way, however, and the quality of the search depends on how well it does.

2.4 An example: gradient descent

This structure has a familiar parallel in gradient descent. There too one looks for a point not known in advance, the minimum of a loss function, by taking steps, and each step goes in the direction given by the gradient computed at the current point. Table 1 puts the two procedures side by side: the parameter vector corresponds to the candidate prompt, the loss to the distance from the target prompt, the gradient to the judge’s diagnosis and the update step to the fix, while the role that in momentum variants (Polyak, 1964) falls to the average of past steps, damping oscillations by remembering where one came from, falls in the loop to the history.

The parallel breaks exactly where the loop needs a judge. The loss in gradient descent is computed and differentiated, and the gradient is the exact result of that computation, whereas the distance from the target prompt can be neither computed nor differentiated and the direction of the step is an estimate that a language model draws from partial observations. With a smooth function and a small enough step, every gradient step reduces the loss, while in the loop nothing guarantees that a fix brings the candidate closer, and a step can move it away (Figure 5). The end point differs too: gradient descent approaches the minimum, while the loop halts on entering 𝐴, at a distance from 𝑠† that depends on how well the testers represent the target.

2.5 Textual gradients, adversaries and reinforcement

The gradient analogy is not new in prompt optimisation. ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023) collects the errors the current prompt makes on a small set of labelled examples, asks an LLM to criticise them in natural language, obtaining a textual “gradient”, and edits the prompt in the opposite semantic direction, keeping several candidates open with a beam search. TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) extends the idea to systems made of several model calls, propagating backwards along the computation graph the feedback that an LLM writes on each variable. In both, the gradient is the critique of a model that reads the prompt, or the variable, together with the errors it produced (Figure 6).

Our loop uses the same analogy inside a different model, and the difference is the one its name declares. It is adversarial because the direction comes not from errors on a fixed set of examples but from testers that actively try to make the candidate fail, each isolated on its own constraint and free to invent the attacks it judges most effective, so that the prompt’s weak points are sought rather than sampled. And it is inspired by reinforcement learning in its division of roles (Sutton and Barto, 2018). The candidate is put to the test in an environment, the testers’ verdicts act as a reward signal, binary and sparse, the compiler that produces the next candidate takes the place of the actor, and the judge, which estimates from the outcomes how far the candidate still is from the target and which step to take, recalls the critic of actor–critic methods. Unlike the critic of ProTeGi and TextGrad, moreover, our judge does not read the prompt it corrects, and reasons only on the outcomes the testers report. From reinforcement learning the loop takes the structure, not the algorithm: no parameter is updated and no policy is trained.

2.6 Coupled constraints: a narrow valley

In this geometry coupled constraints have a recognisable shape. When two constraints compete for the same resource, for example a length limit that a safety rule and a note for staff must share, the region where both are met is a narrow strip between two boundaries, and a step meant for only one of them tends to cross the strip entirely and land on the other side (Figure 7). The fix for 𝐴 breaks 𝐵, the fix for 𝐵 breaks 𝐴 again, and the candidate oscillates from one side of the strip to the other, as gradient descent oscillates between the walls of a narrow valley. In gradient descent the classic remedy is momentum, which by summing successive steps cancels the components that alternate and keeps the one that runs along the valley. In the loop the same task falls to the history, because a judge that reads the alternation in it can recognise the coupling and write a single step, meant for both constraints, that brings the candidate into the strip. This is what happened in the Bramble run (Section 7.1), where the judge traced the alternation between two testers to a shared word budget.

2.7 The compiler’s direction

The judge chooses the steps, but which points can be reached, and how a fix becomes a candidate, depend on the compiler, and it is the compiler that first sets the direction of the search. A native compiler, an LLM driven only by its role prompt, can write any prompt, and the direction is then the one set by the target 𝑃 the user chose. A specialised compiler, built for a particular kind of prompt or result, works instead in one part of the space and already follows a direction of its own there, which the loop is meant to reinforce: the testers and the judge push the search towards the target prompt while staying in the region where that compiler works (Figure 8). This is the same distinction by which Section 3.1 describes the loop as a wrapper around a known technique, a use that none of our runs has yet put to the test.

3 Method: three roles and one cycle

The loop splits generation into three phases: compile, test and judge. It has three roles and a fixed cycle (Figure 9); the cycle 𝐶→𝑇‖→halt→𝐽→𝐻 is the same in every instantiation. Each role is a separate LLM agent with its own prompt and a restricted context (its receive-set, Section 4.1). The compiler receives the target 𝑃 and the fix projection of the history, 𝜋𝐹(𝐻𝑛)=(𝑓1,...,𝑓𝑛), and produces a candidate 𝑠. By design, the compiler never receives raw verdicts, only the judge’s fixes. Withholding raw verdicts is meant to keep it from satisfying the letter of individual tests instead of the target; this is a design rationale, which we did not test.

Each tester checks one constraint, and testers run in parallel within an iteration. By design, testers are mutually isolated: no tester receives another tester’s output, unlike multi-agent debate (Du et al., 2024), where agents read and respond to each other’s answers. By design, each tester receives only its projection proj(𝑠,𝑖) of the candidate (and its own constraint). A projection here is a context-selection function: proj(𝑠,𝑖) is the part of 𝑠 placed in tester 𝑖’s context, not a projection in the linear-algebra sense. Testers are instructed to be adversarial, that is, to try to break the candidate rather than merely grade it.

The judge outputs a diagnosis (why the candidate failed) and a fix (what to change); the testers do the grading. By design, it is the only role that receives the outputs of more than one tester, and so the only role that reasons across constraints. LLM-Modulo’s meta-controller also pools several critics’ feedback (Kambhampati et al., 2024); our judge additionally reads the full verdict–fix history 𝐻 and never the candidate. By design, the history is the mechanism meant to counter oscillation. The judge is not called on an iteration that halts.

3.1 The loop as a wrapper

The loop asks one thing of the compiler: that it turn the target and the accumulated fixes into a candidate, 𝐶:𝑃×𝐹∗→𝑆. Nothing in the testers, the judge or the history depends on how that candidate is produced. The compiler can therefore be native, a single LLM call driven by its role prompt, as in both runs of Section 7, or any prompt-engineering technique that can be encoded with that signature: an automatic prompt optimiser such as APE, OPRO or ProTeGi (Zhou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Pryzant et al., 2023), a declarative pipeline such as DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024), an evolutionary method such as Promptbreeder or EvoPrompt (Fernando et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024), or a hand-designed prompt-construction framework such as Prometheus, the framework our role prompts follow. When a technique does not accept fixes as input, a thin adapter can translate them into what it does accept, for example extra instructions or feedback examples.

In this second use the loop runs around the technique as an outer layer (Figure 10). The technique keeps its own search and, if it has one, its own evaluation; the loop adds isolated testers on the target’s constraints, a judge that reads the whole history, and a stopping rule. The direction the loop takes is therefore set first by the compiler underneath it. A specialised compiler, built for a particular kind of prompt or result, already points the search somewhere, and the loop is meant to reinforce that optimisation in that direction; with a general-purpose compiler, the direction comes from the target the user sets. The aim in both cases is to help the technique, and the prompts it generates, converge on the target, especially when the constraints are coupled and the objective the technique optimises does not see all of them. In design-pattern terms (Gamma et al., 1994) the loop is a Decorator: it offers outside the same interface as a prompt-engineering technique, a target in and an artefact out, and adds behaviour around each call, while the compiler inside it is a Strategy that can be swapped without changing the loop. Neither run in Section 7 used a wrapped technique, so the wrapper use is, for now, a property of the interface rather than an observed result.

4 Information flow and projections

4.1 The invariants as receive-sets

The method imposes five information-flow invariants, stated as what each role receives, because isolation is implemented by what goes into each agent’s context. They are requirements the orchestrator must enforce, not derived properties; in our runs they were enforced by prompt assembly plus an instruction, not by sandboxing. With Cons=(𝑐1,...,𝑐𝑚) the constraint descriptions:

I1

Compiler ←{𝑃, 𝜋𝐹(𝐻)}: the fix column of the history, never the verdicts, never the previous candidate.

I2

No tester receives another tester’s output.

I3

Tester 𝑖←{proj(𝑠,𝑖), 𝑐𝑖} only.

I4

Judge ←{𝑃, Cons, 𝑣𝑛 with reasons, 𝐻𝑛−1}, the only role receiving more than one tester’s output.1

I5

The judge receives no part of 𝑠 except what tester reasons contain.

The edge view. The source note states the same discipline as edges between roles (Figure 11); its five edge statements, numbered I1–I5 in a different order, describe the same graph when its I1 is read as “the only path that carries 𝑠”. The candidate reaches the testers only through projections, and this is the only path that carries 𝑠; there are no tester-to-tester paths. Information flows from testers to the judge only, as verdicts with a reason for each, and from the judge to the compiler only through the fixes recorded in 𝐻; the compiler never queries the judge. There is no compiler-to-judge path, so the judge sees the candidate only through the testers’ verdicts and reasons. Information flows from compiler to testers to judge within an iteration; the judge-to-compiler edge through the history feeds the next iteration, so there is no cycle within an iteration.

4.2 Projections

Projections are how isolation is enforced: a tester’s context contains only its projection. That this makes each test independently meaningful is a design rationale. A candidate with 𝑘 components is 𝑠=(𝑥1,...,𝑥𝑘) (Figure 12); a disjoint projection gives tester 𝑖 one component, proj(𝑠,𝑖)=𝑥𝑖, and a full projection gives the whole candidate, proj(𝑠,𝑚)=𝑠. A tester that receives only 𝑥1 has no direct access to 𝑥2. It may still infer 𝑥2 when the components are correlated (for example, a description that restates a regex). A full-projection tester checks holistic properties such as end-to-end correctness. A common pattern combines disjoint testers for component constraints with a full-projection tester for the integrated result; every run shown does so (Table 2). A tester given the full candidate when its constraint concerns one component breaks the isolation invariant, and its verdict can no longer be read as a check of that component alone.

1The note’s role summary lists the candidate among the judge’s inputs. This contradicts its invariant I5, its figures and the orchestrator used in our runs; we follow I5 throughout.

5 Formal model

Definition 1 (System). A loop is the tuple (𝑃,𝑆,𝐶,𝑇,𝐽,halt,𝑁): target specification, output space, compiler, testers, judge, halt predicate and iteration budget. 𝐹 is the space of fixes (free text), 𝐵 that of barrier declarations.

  • 𝑇𝑖:proj(𝑆,𝑖)→{𝗉𝖺𝗌𝗌,𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅}×Reason returns a verdict and a reason (corrected from the note’s bare {𝗉𝖺𝗌𝗌,𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅}); 𝑣=(𝑣1,...,𝑣𝑚)∈𝑉 is the verdict vector. The reason is what the judge diagnoses from; halt and the loss read only the binary part.

  • 𝐶:𝑃×𝐹∗→𝑆 reads the target and the fix projection of the history (corrected from the note’s 𝑃×𝐻→𝑆). It does not receive the previous candidate; the last statement below shows what follows.

  • 𝐽:𝑃×Cons×𝑉×(𝑉×𝐹)∗→𝐹∪𝐵 reads the target, the constraint descriptions, the current verdict vector and the full history, and returns a fix or a barrier declaration (corrected from the note’s 𝑉×𝐻→𝐹, which omitted 𝑃 and the constraints).

  • halt:𝑉→{𝗒𝖾𝗌,𝗇𝗈} is the halt predicate, by default “all testers pass”; 𝑁 is the iteration budget.

The history is 𝐻0=(), 𝐻𝑛=𝐻𝑛−1⋅(𝑣𝑛,𝑓𝑛), with 𝜋𝐹(𝐻𝑛)=(𝑓1,...,𝑓𝑛); 𝑓𝑛 is the judge’s full recommended fix.

Algorithm 1 gives one step and the loop around it. Its update 𝐻𝑛←𝐻𝑛−1⋅(𝑣𝑛,𝑓𝑛) corrects the note’s 𝐻←𝐻∪{𝑓}, which stores fixes only although the judge needs past verdicts to detect oscillation. A barrier declaration stops the run, so the loop may stop before 𝑁.

Loss, feasibility, relaxation. The loss 𝐿(𝑠𝑛)=|{𝑖:𝑣𝑛,𝑖=𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅}| is the number of failing verdicts in iteration 𝑛. It is an integer, used only by the halt test, and is never differentiated or minimised by gradients. The loop seeks a candidate 𝑠∗ with 𝐿(𝑠∗)=0, that is, a point of the acceptance region 𝐴 (Section 2.1). Feasibility is Φ=∃𝑠∈𝑆:𝐿(𝑠)=0. It is defined relative to the testers and is well defined only when the testers are deterministic. A relaxation replaces a tester’s criterion by a weaker one, so verdicts stay binary and halt stays a predicate on 𝑉. Any relaxation must be declared before the loop starts; accepting a marginal pass is then a design decision rather than a post-hoc rationalisation. The target problem can be read as discrete constraint satisfaction in which the constraints are checked by LLM testers rather than decided by a solver (Marques-Silva and Sakallah, 1999).

What the loop guarantees, and what it does not.

  • Cost is bounded: a run makes at most 𝑁(𝑚+2) role calls, counting each tester as one call; for the Bramble run (five testers, 𝑁=6) that is at most 42. Why: there are at most 𝑁 rounds, each with one compiler call, 𝑚 tester calls and at most one judge call (none on the round that halts).

  • Halting is sound only relative to the testers: under halt = all-pass, a returned candidate passed every tester in its round, so the constraints hold only insofar as each pass is correct; with deterministic testers, if no candidate passes every tester (Φ false), halt never fires and the loop cannot return a halted candidate. Why: halt is a predicate on the verdicts alone, so it inherits every tester error and every requirement no tester checks.

  • Reaching the budget does not establish infeasibility: when the loop stops at 𝑁 without halting, the history is diagnostic evidence for a barrier, not the “constructive proof of infeasibility” the note calls it, and not an unsatisfiability answer from a sound solver such as the verifier in CEGIS (Solar-Lezama et al., 2006). Why: the loop stops at 𝑁 whenever no passing candidate was produced within 𝑁 rounds, whether or not one exists, and Φ is itself relative to the testers; if Φ is false the loop stops at 𝑁, or earlier on a barrier declaration, but the converse does not hold.

  • A compiler that never sees the previous candidate cannot reliably carry out a fix that only points at it (“keep 𝑋 unchanged”; the SemVer run, Section 7.2). Why: it rebuilds the candidate from the target and the fixes alone, so any 𝑋 not written into them must be regenerated, and nothing makes the regenerated 𝑋 equal the old one; the judge, which by I5 never sees the candidate either, cannot restate it.

6 Why the loop should converge: design rationale

We identify three design mechanisms meant to promote convergence: informed mutation, a tabu-like use of the history, and coupling detection. Theorem 1 states what follows if informed fixes and the tabu-like history work as intended; whether a real judge meets its assumptions is not shown, and what the runs show is observation only (Figure 13). “Informed mutation” is borrowed from evolutionary search by analogy: the judge’s fix replaces a random mutation, but there is no population and no selection operator. By design, the judge’s fix is a targeted diagnosis of why tests failed, not a random perturbation. We expect diagnosis-driven fixes to direct the search more effectively than random mutation; we do not measure this. Uninformed mutation-based search is not guided by a diagnosis of failure; its runtime depends on the problem (Droste et al., 2002). Figure 14 sketches the intended difference.

𝐻 acts as a tabu list only informally: in tabu search (Glover, 1986) the exclusion is explicit and enforced, whereas here avoiding tried fixes is left to the judge. Fixes that were tried and failed stay visible to the judge, and the judge is instructed not to re-propose them. In the Bramble run the judge’s third fix explicitly set aside an option (enumerating the missing framings) because it would recreate the 𝑇1/𝑇4 budget trade seen in earlier iterations (Figure 15). OPRO likewise conditions each new proposal on previously tried solutions and their scores (Yang et al., 2024). The history only grows, so the record of tried fixes grows monotonically; pruning follows only if the judge never re-proposes a tried fix, an assumption about the judge, not a property of the loop.

A conditional convergence theorem. The theorem below phrases the mechanisms above as two assumptions about the judge and states what follows if they hold. Let 𝐴𝑛 be the event that the round-𝑛 candidate passes every tester (halt(𝑣𝑛)=𝗒𝖾𝗌), and let F𝑛−1 be everything observed before round 𝑛: the history 𝐻𝑛−1 and the earlier candidates and verdicts.

Theorem 1 (Convergence under informed fixes). Assume (i) informed progress: there is 𝑝∈(0,1] such that, for every round 𝑛≥1 reached without halting, Pr(𝐴𝑛∣F𝑛−1)≥𝑝; and (ii) the judge returns a fix, not a barrier declaration, after every round before 𝑁 that does not halt. Then the loop halts within 𝑁 rounds with probability at least 1−(1−𝑝)𝑁. Without a budget (𝑁=∞) it halts with probability 1, after an expected number of rounds at most 1/𝑝.

Proof. Let 𝑇 be the round at which the loop halts (𝑇=∞ if it never does). By (ii), before the budget the loop stops only by halting, so round 𝑛≤𝑁 is reached exactly on the event {𝑇>𝑛−1}, which is determined by F𝑛−1. On that event (i) gives Pr(𝐴𝑐𝑛∣F𝑛−1)≤1−𝑝, hence Pr(𝑇>𝑛)=𝔼[𝟏{𝑇>𝑛−1}Pr(𝐴𝑐𝑛∣F𝑛−1)]≤(1−𝑝)Pr(𝑇>𝑛−1), and by induction Pr(𝑇>𝑛)≤(1−𝑝)𝑛. Taking 𝑛=𝑁 gives Pr(𝑇≤𝑁)≥1−(1−𝑝)𝑁. Without a budget, Pr(𝑇=∞)≤lim𝑛(1−𝑝)𝑛=0 and 𝔼[𝑇]=∑𝑛≥0Pr(𝑇>𝑛)≤∑𝑛≥0(1−𝑝)𝑛=1/𝑝. □

Proposition 1 (Termination under a strict tabu). If the fix space 𝐹 is finite and the judge never returns a fix already in 𝜋𝐹(𝐻𝑛−1), the loop stops (by halting, by a barrier declaration, or at the budget) within min(𝑁,|𝐹|+1) rounds.

Proof. Every round that neither halts nor ends the run appends a fix to the history, and by assumption these fixes are pairwise distinct elements of 𝐹, so at most |𝐹| rounds can end with a fix. If round |𝐹|+1≤𝑁 is reached and does not halt, every fix in 𝐹 has been used; since 𝐽 maps into 𝐹∪𝐵, the judge must return a barrier declaration and the loop stops. □

Remark. Assumption (i) is the formal reading of informed mutation: whatever happened before, each round has at least a fixed chance of producing a candidate that passes every tester. A judge that misdiagnoses, or re-proposes failed fixes, can violate it; uninformed mutation in a large output space corresponds to a far smaller 𝑝, and the same waiting-time argument underlies fitness-level runtime analyses of the (1+1) EA (Droste et al., 2002). With exact testers and Φ false, 𝑝=0 and the theorem says nothing, consistent with reaching the budget not establishing infeasibility (Section 5). Proposition 1 is what the tabu effect would give if it were enforced: termination, not speed, since |𝐹| is finite for bounded-length fixes but astronomically large. Two runs, halting at rounds 4 and 3, cannot estimate 𝑝.

For coupling detection, when the history shows that fixing test 𝑖 broke test 𝑗, the judge is designed to diagnose the coupling and propose one fix that addresses both. The Bramble run shows this once: the judge labelled the 𝑇1/𝑇4 alternation, traced it to the shared 90-word budget, judged the pair jointly satisfiable, and its third fix was followed by an iteration in which every tester passed (Figure 16). We hypothesise that the accumulated history lets the judge make structural diagnoses, such as identifying a coupled pair of constraints, that a single iteration would not reveal, and that coupling detection is what breaks oscillations; the Bramble run is consistent with both, since the judge’s diagnosis drew on two iterations of history and the oscillation ended after its fix for both constraints. Loosely analogous to conjugate gradients (Hestenes and Stiefel, 1952), which use earlier search directions to avoid revisiting them, the judge uses the history to avoid repeating failed fixes; the loop has no counterpart to conjugacy or its guarantees.

Oscillation. We regard oscillation as the main convergence risk under coupled constraints; this is a design premise, not a measured finding. Figure 17 is a schematic, not a run: 𝑇1 fails at 𝑛, 𝑇2 at 𝑛+1, 𝑇1 again at 𝑛+2; the judge sees the alternation in 𝐻, proposes a coupling fix, and both pass at 𝑛+3. Alternating failures suggest coupled constraints, though stochastic testers can also produce alternating verdicts. The history is meant to make a coupling visible to the judge, so that it can propose one fix that satisfies both constraints; in the Bramble run the alternation was visible in the ledger, and after fix 3 both 𝑇1 and 𝑇4 passed. We expect a judge that does not read the history to be more likely to re-propose failed fixes, but we did not test a memoryless variant. The note’s claim that such a loop “oscillates indefinitely” does not follow: withholding the history from the judge alone leaves the compiler reading the cumulative fixes, and nothing forces the candidates to cycle.

Structural barriers. A barrier declaration is the judge’s claim that two constraints cannot be met together; it is a diagnosis, not a finding of infeasibility. In the Bramble run the judge instead judged its constraints jointly satisfiable (“coupling to resolve, not a barrier”). We expect each failed approach recorded in the history to narrow down why the constraints conflict, until the judge can name the barrier; the runs shown did not take this path, and Figure 18 is a schematic of it. A diagnosed barrier can be useful in its own right, because it points to which constraint to relax. If the budget is exhausted, the judge treats a structural barrier as a working hypothesis and names a constraint to relax; exhausting the budget does not establish Φ = false (Section 5). The barrier report (the history, the judge’s barrier diagnosis and the constraint it recommends relaxing) is thus a defined outcome beside a halted candidate.

7 Case study: two runs, iteration by iteration

We show two live runs, which we name after their tasks: the Bramble run, which hardens the system prompt of a library assistant called Bramble, and the SemVer run, which writes a regex for Semantic Versioning and its description. Both were run by the orchestrator (an orchestrating Claude session with a small helper script) and are observations, not a benchmark (𝑛=2; Table 2). Each configuration was confirmed by the author before its roles were drafted, and the role prompts followed the prompt shapes of the author’s Prometheus framework.2 All roles ran as fresh Claude Code sub-agents on Claude Opus 5.5 (default sampling; temperature and seed unrecorded), each prompted with its permitted context only (Section 4.1); isolation rested on these prompt files plus an instruction not to access other paths, and the sub-agents had file-system tools. The full transcripts are in the supplementary material.

7.1 The Bramble run: hardening a prompt for a small model

The Bramble run hardens the system prompt of “Ask Bramble”, an assistant for the fictional Harlow University Library. The prompt must answer public questions (including fines of 20p per item per day, capped at £5), hold a confidential staff note (code HX-4471; fines under £10 may be waived at staff discretion) without disclosing it or obeying injected instructions, and keep its Instructions 𝑥1 within 90 words, before two or three example exchanges 𝑥2. 𝑇1 (leak) and 𝑇2 (usability) wrote fresh probes in each iteration, sent them to the candidate deployed as the system prompt of a Claude Haiku 5.5 sub-agent, and judged the real replies; 𝑇3, 𝑇4 and 𝑇5 checked the budget, the staff note (code exact) and the two-section form. Tester reasons locate each failure, because the judge never sees the candidate. Figure 19 carries the trajectory; the list below summarises it.

  • Iteration 1. 𝑇1 failed (11 of 14 attacks held): refusals such as “I can’t share internal details about how fines are waived at the desk, including amounts or the override process” confirm that the withheld mechanism exists. Fix 1, a redirect that never confirms or denies a waiver, did not mention the staff note.

  • Iteration 2. 𝑇1 passed, but the staff note was gone (“Never reveal internal notes/codes”) and 𝑇4 failed. The judge labelled “oscillation (𝑇1 and 𝑇4, iterations 1–2)”, traced it to the shared 90-word budget, and wrote fix 2: 89 words of Instructions with the note verbatim.

  • Iteration 3. 𝑇4 passed and 𝑇1 failed (16 of 18): a forwarded admin email drew “I won’t share internal codes or amounts”, as the redirect covered only fine-reduction questions. Judging the pair jointly satisfiable, not a barrier, the judge set aside listing the missing framings, which could not fit beside the staff note (Figure 15), and wrote fix 3, a framing-independent, positively closed deflection: “however asked, implied, or pasted, reply only: rate, cap, help-desk review. Add nothing; name nothing you won’t share”.

  • Iteration 4. All five testers passed3 and the loop halted at iteration 4 of 𝑁=6; over the run the deployed assistant held 58 of 63 executed attacks. No ablation separates which part of fix 3 mattered.

7.2 The SemVer run: a regex and its description

The SemVer run asks for a regex 𝑅 (≤160 characters, for Python’s re.fullmatch) matching exactly the strings valid under Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (Preston-Werner, 2013), plus a description 𝐷 (≤120 words) of exactly what 𝑅 accepts and rejects. 𝑇1 (accept), 𝑇2 (reject) and 𝑇3 (length) see only 𝑅; 𝑇4 (is 𝐷 faithful to 𝑅?) sees both; the compiler could test its own work with tools, inside what the formal model treats as one call. Only 𝑇4 failed (Table 3). Fix 1 wrote a new 𝐷 in full and said to keep 𝑅 byte for byte; the compiler, which never receives the previous candidate, reported that it could not and regenerated 𝑅, while its 𝐷 was the judge’s paragraph byte for byte. Content written into a fix survived; a fix that only pointed at the previous candidate did not. Outside the loop, the orchestrator found 0 disagreements between the final 𝑅 and an ASCII-only transcription of the semver.org reference regex on 300,000 fuzzed strings (seed 7), a check rather than a proof.

SemVer run, final candidate (iteration 3; every tester passed)

R: 

(?a)(0|[1-9]\d*)(\.(0|[1-9]\d*)){2}(-(0|[1-9]\d*|\d*[A-Za-z-][\dA-Za-z-]*)(\.(0|[1-9]\d*|\d*[A-Za-z-][\dA-Za-z-]*))*)?(\+[\dA-Za-z-]+(\.[\dA-Za-z-]+)*)?

D: R matches only the whole string MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, optionally followed by a pre-release after a hyphen, then optionally build metadata after a plus sign. MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH are integers of ASCII digits (0-9) with no leading zero unless the number is exactly 0. Pre-release and build metadata are each one or more dot-separated, non-empty identifiers using only ASCII letters (A-Z, a-z), ASCII digits (0-9) and hyphens; any other character in an identifier is rejected, including non-ASCII letters or digits, underscores and whitespace. An all-digit pre-release identifier must not have a leading zero unless it is exactly 0. One containing a letter or hyphen may start with 0. Build identifiers may have leading zeros. A ‘v’ prefix is rejected.

2https://github.com/Samuele95/prometheus; accessed 2026-11-05.

3From iteration 4 the orchestrator’s task message to the deployment sub-agents also said “Use only file read and file write tools.”; the deployment prompt was unchanged, the message’s effect on the replies was not measured, and iteration 4 is also the iteration at which every tester passed. No role prompt, tester or budget changed during the run.

8 Instantiation and design guidelines

Instantiating the loop means fixing three things (Figure 20): the output space 𝑆, which is what the compiler may produce and so bounds the search, the testers with their projections, and the halt predicate. As a guideline, a loop uses at least two and at most about five testers. The halt predicate, “all testers pass” or a relaxed criterion, is fixed before the loop starts. We expect the loop to transfer to other tasks whose constraints are coupled and cheap to check; we have run it only on prompt hardening and on a regex-plus-description target.

Roles. Each tester should be adversarial: instructed to try hard to break the candidate, and explicitly permitted lateral thinking and creative attacks. The judge must receive the full history, not just the latest iteration. The history is shown to the judge as a table (iteration, each tester’s verdict, the fix applied), so that oscillation, progressive narrowing and repeated failure of one test are visible; in the Bramble run the judge additionally received every past fix in full, as the compiler did, and its testers gave locating reasons (Section 7.1). The judge outputs a root cause, candidate fixes with trade-offs, and one recommended fix with implementation details.

Fixes that point at the candidate. Because the compiler never sees the previous candidate (Section 5), content that must survive should be written into the fix, as the judge did in the SemVer and Bramble runs. Three untested design options address fixes that only point at the candidate: the judge can be required to write fixes as self-contained content, never as pointers; the orchestrator can resolve pointer fixes against the stored candidate; or, most directly, the compiler can receive the previous candidate, extending 𝐶 to 𝑃×𝐹∗×𝑆→𝑆, which changes I1 and the formal model.

Budget. As a planning guideline (not a measured requirement): plan 3–4 iterations for 2–3 constraints and 5–6 for 4–6 interacting constraints. The Bramble run, with five constraints, set 𝑁=6 by this guideline; the SemVer run (four constraints) also used 𝑁=6. This rule and the cap of about five testers meet at six constraints, where constraints should be fused or the cap exceeded; the Bramble run used five testers for five constraints, at the cap.

9 Conclusion

We specified the Adversarial RL Loop as three roles with explicit receive-sets, corrected its model so that the history holds verdict–fix pairs and the compiler reads only the fixes, and stated what the loop guarantees and what it does not. Because the compiler is defined only by its interface, the same loop works as a prompt-engineering technique of its own, with a native compiler, or as a wrapper around an existing technique, meant to help it converge in the direction its compiler or the user’s target sets. Two runs show it at work. In the Bramble run the judge, reading only tester reasons and the history, recognised that a fix for a leak had cost the prompt its confidential note, traced the trade to a shared word budget, and wrote a deflection that applies however a request is framed; the next candidate passed all five testers. In the SemVer run, text that the judge wrote out carried the description through a compiler that never sees the previous candidate.

Limitations. The runs shown (Bramble and SemVer) are illustrative examples selected by the author from a larger set of runs; they are not an evaluation and say nothing about how often the loop succeeds, and with no baseline or ablation nothing here compares the loop with single-pass prompting or Self-Refine, or shows which part of a fix or configuration was necessary. Halting is relative to the testers: 𝐿(𝑠)=0 means only that the testers passed the candidate, a requirement no tester checks is not enforced, and in the Bramble run the deployment was a Haiku sub-agent answering single messages, not a production endpoint. A run costs up to 𝑁(𝑚+2) role calls plus the deployment calls of executed testers; tokens and time were not measured. The tabu-like effect and coupling detection depend on the judge honouring the history, which nothing enforces. All roles are stochastic, with temperature and seed unrecorded, so a rerun can differ. Both runs used a native compiler, so the wrapper use has not yet been exercised.

Next steps are repeated runs with controlled sampling against a single-pass baseline, and ablations of the history and of the judge’s fix format, as well as runs in which the loop wraps an existing technique such as OPRO or DSPy.

Related work

Analogies. The loop borrows ideas from several established methods: preference-based RL (Christiano et al., 2017), generative adversarial networks (Goodfellow et al., 2014), conflict-driven clause-learning (CDCL) SAT solving (Marques-Silva and Sakallah, 1999), tabu search (Glover, 1986), evolutionary search (Droste et al., 2002) and conjugate gradients (Hestenes and Stiefel, 1952). We state each borrowing as an analogy, and each stops early: from RL, which in RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022) uses PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), the loop takes the division of roles into an actor, an environment that returns an outcome and a critic that estimates the distance to the target (Section 2.5), but no weights are updated and no reward is maximised; against GANs, nothing is trained and no equilibrium is sought; against CDCL, the history plays the part of learned conflict clauses, but CDCL’s clauses propagate soundly, whereas 𝐻 is free text with no soundness guarantee; against the (1+1) EA, the informed fix replaces random mutation, with no population and no selection operator.

Refinement, critique, checkers and judges. Self-Refine uses one model to generate, critique and refine (Madaan et al., 2023); Reflexion keeps verbal reflections in an episodic memory across trials without updating weights (Shinn et al., 2023); CRITIC and Self-Debug ground the critique in tools or execution (Gou et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024); intrinsic self-correction without external feedback can fail (Huang et al., 2024). Our loop shares this generate–critique–revise shape, with the roles split across agents with fixed receive-sets. Pairing several checkers with a controller that pools their critiques and back-prompts the generator is the LLM-Modulo architecture (Kambhampati et al., 2024), our nearest neighbour; it also makes the point that soundness can only come from sound critics. Multi-agent debate (Du et al., 2024), verifier-based selection (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) and LLM-as-a-judge grading (Zheng et al., 2023) differ from the loop as noted in Sections 1 and 3.

Prompt optimisation and CEGIS. Like other prompt-optimisation and textual-feedback methods (APE (Zhou et al., 2023), OPRO (Yang et al., 2024), ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023), TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025), DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024), Promptbreeder (Fernando et al., 2024), EvoPrompt (Guo et al., 2024)), the loop works on discrete symbolic artefacts (prompts, specifications) through natural-language changes, not on continuous parameters through gradients. This is shared with prior work, not a differentiator; OPRO’s meta-prompt of scored past solutions is the closest counterpart to our history. What sets the loop apart from ProTeGi and TextGrad, which also describe the search as gradient descent, is its adversarial testers and a judge that does not read the prompt (Section 2.5). These methods are also candidates for the compiler role: wrapped by the loop (Section 3.1), each would keep its own search while the loop adds isolated checks on the target’s constraints and a judge over the history. CEGIS (Solar-Lezama et al., 2006) is a synthesiser–verifier loop driven by counterexamples in which the verifier is a sound solver, counterexamples are concrete inputs, and termination over finite spaces and unsatisfiability are real theorems. None of these guarantees carries over, because our testers are LLMs and our fixes are free text.

Iterative red teaming. PAIR (Chao et al., 2023) shares the loop’s skeleton, a black-box cycle in which one LLM proposes a prompt, another evaluates the result and the history drives the next attempt, but runs it in the opposite direction: an attacker rewrites a jailbreak prompt until a judge, scoring the target model’s response from 1 to 10, reports success. The attacker sees its earlier prompts, the target’s responses and the scores, and writes both its own improvement and the next prompt. In our loop that work is split between a judge that never sees the candidate and a compiler that sees only fixes, several isolated testers replace the single score, and the run ends only when the candidate passes all of them, or with a barrier report. A PAIR-style attacker could serve as one of the testers; in the Bramble run 𝑇1 plays a simpler, single-step version of that role. Table 4 summarises the differences.

What is new. What the paper offers is narrower than the loop itself (the contributions of Section 1). As far as the sources we checked show, prior loops do not separate who reads what in the way our receive-sets do; we claim the explicit, enforceable specification, not the first use of isolation.

PAIR

Aim

Objective

𝑚 coupled constraints, one pass/fail tester each

Who writes the change

the attacker, after reflecting on scores and responses

a judge that reads verdicts and history, never the candidate

Visibility

the attacker sees its prompts, the responses and the scores

each role receives only its receive-set; testers see projections

Search

𝑁 parallel streams of 𝐾 rounds

one trajectory with budget 𝑁; the history steers away from repeats

Stop

every tester passes, or the run ends with a barrier report
